If one more audio brand releases earbuds/headphones with "AI features", I'm going to scream.

And, as it turns out, so will 98% of Tom's Guide readers. Or, put bluntly, so will you. Of 200 responses, only five readers said they specifically look for AI features in the best earbuds and best headphones. Most readers voted sound quality as their most important feature: 135 people, specifically. ANC came second with twenty-seven votes. Yes, first place received five times as many votes as second place.

This got me thinking: Why? Why do audio brands keep pushing AI features down our throats when we so clearly don't want them? Do said brands worry they'll be "left behind" in the AI race? Do brands consider sound quality, ANC, and call quality last year's news? Or is it something else...? Let's dig in.

I ran a poll for three weeks here on Tom's Guide. I asked, and you all answered! Here are the exact results.

As you can see, sound quality is by far the most important feature for you. ANC came second with 13% of the vote, then call quality and other came joint third with 6% of the vote. Second-to-last we have battery life, 4% of the vote. And, trailing last, we have AI features — with just 2% of the vote.

I could've predicted that sound quality would win, but I was genuinely surprised when I saw AI features lost by that much. I thought it would get more like... maybe 10%. I thought some people really liked having AI in earbuds, but evidently not.

I loved the Anker Soundcore Space One Pro headphones. They were my biggest surprise of 2025 and I ended up recommending them to pretty much everyone. I even got my sister a pair for college! They're the perfect headphones for studying thanks to the incredible ANC, comfort, and foldability.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I feel like Anker put so much effort into AI features, it forgot what the Soundcore Space 2 Pro were: headphones. For music. And ANC. Not glorified chatbot earmuffs.

So when I reviewed the successor, Space 2 Pro, they left me with a sour taste in my mouth. This was especially sour because I wasn't expecting it. I was expecting another Space One Pro: slam-dunk, instant favorite. But it wasn't.

The reason? The AI features. I feel like Anker put so much effort into AI features, it forgot what the Soundcore Space 2 Pro were: headphones. For music. And ANC. Not glorified chatbot earmuffs.

Don't get me wrong, I still awarded the Space 2 Pro 3.5 stars — this means "very good." And the headphones are very good. Sound quality is great, call quality is great, and ANC is great. Triple whammy there... as long as you ignore the purported AI functionality in the Anker app.

Let me set the scene: the Soundcore Space 2 Pro are advertised as having the "world's first neural-net compute-in-memory AI audio chip". If you don't know what that means, you're not alone!

Amanda Caswell, AI Editor here at Tom's Guide, translated this into real terms. "AI-powered audio processing inside that's efficient enough to run continuously on a tiny, battery-powered device.

"So this could help with smarter noise cancellation, voice isolation, always-on listening (to detect words). But "neural-net" is the chip that runs artificial neural networks trained to recognize and process sounds, such as speech, background noise and potentially voice commands."

And there's a lovely chatbot in the Anker Soundcore app! However, Anker's marketing doesn't actually specify that the Space 2 Pro are compatible with the in-app chatbot. Might it be my fault that I assumed the app features would work?

If I connect headphones to my phone, download the companion app, open the companion app, see a big "AI chatbot!" tab that can supposedly adjust my EQ in real-time, I'd assume it works, right?

Take a look at this. These are real screenshots from the Anker app.

When I asked Anker's representative about this, I was told, "Currently, Anka on Space 2 Pro only supports activation via “Hey Anka” and basic voice interactions or chats.

Other features, including voice controls, audio playback and text-based interactions in the app, are still in development, not ready for release."

So why are the features present in the app? I've been in further contact with Anker, which has informed me it is looking into the issue — so that's a win!

But the most frustrating part is this: I don't actually care if headphones or earbuds have (useless to me) AI features or not. I won't mark down audio products for simply including things like Live Translation — if it works, it's actually a huge plus, like with the AirPods Max 2 or Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

When I reviewed the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max, which can accurately transcribe calls and meetings directly to the app, I gave them four stars and our coveted Recommended badge.

So what was different with the Space 2 Pro, then? Same audio brand, same AI features, right?

The Liberty 5 Pro Max's AI features actually worked. If the AI features work, regardless of my personal dislike of AI, I mark it as a positive and go on about my day. I don't write a 2,000-word long-read about the state of AI in earbuds and headphones (...).

The Space 2 Pro sound amazing. They don't need any gimmicky AI features. If Anker had positioned them as straightforward, comfy, great-ANC wireless headphones, they'd have received a 4.5-star rating.

Now let's go to the opposite side of the earbud/headphone coin: the Cambridge Audio Melomania A100 SE.

The Melomania A100 SE came out in October 2026. I loved these earbuds enough to award them four stars and the sought-after "Tom's Guide recommended" badge. The sound quality is supreme, they're comfy, and they have excellent battery life. The only thing holding them back is the mediocre ANC, but if you're not part of that 13% of readers who prioritize ANC, this shouldn't be an issue.

And the best part — they're just $149. At that price point, there's not much competition. Naturally, there's the AirPods 5 at $129/$149 or the Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 at $149, but the Melomania A100 SE are (literally) music to my ears. Pardon the cliché, but I said what I said.

Michael Laws, a product manager from Cambridge Audio, doesn't seem to think the Melomania A100 SE need AI. "We haven’t put resource into implementing AI features, because so far we haven’t found it’s a requirement when listening to your favourite music on the go. That’s not to say we won’t explore further if there prove to be ways in which, for instance, AI can “help” with different listening profiles."

I completely agree. AI is not a requirement at all. There's a reason why wired audio gear is making a comeback. Consumers are literally rejecting AI being forced into every aspect of our lives. Just this year, Sony has relaunched its original Walkman headphones, and Bose is releasing wired earbuds.

I don't think it's a coincidence. I think people are voting with their wallets, and showing audio brands what they really want.

"One thing that always gets commented on is the sound; that’s our bread and butter," said Cambridge Audio's Laws.

For me, too, sound is my bread and butter. I would much rather have earbuds and headphones that make my music sound alive than a chatbot built into the app — that doesn't even work.

I'm not saying these AI features can't be useful. Live Translation would be useful if it worked, but it's too slow to benefit real-time conversations. On top of that. we've coexisted with machine learning since the '70s — autofocus is machine learning. DSPs in various audio products, from mics to earbuds, use machine learning.

But what is new is a generative AI chatbot in my headphones' companion app. And I'm so over it. If this trend continues, I'll switch to Bose's new Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds (whenever they come back in stock).

Read Ralph Earle’s poem from the November 2026 issue

After retiring from IBM as a senior software engineer in 2017, Ralph Earle has published two poetry collections.

I step into the warm moist airamong the columns of the pines,their net of twigs and rootscomplex as any lines of code.

The trees purify and anchor.Their branches balance my restlessness.

Their calling is to be present,mine to develop apps. Our tasksverge toward a common logic:living filaments of root, of interface.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. While at IBM, he coauthored Enterprise Computing with Objects: From Client/Server Environments to the Internet for Addison-Wesley’s Bloch-Jacobson-Rumbaugh Object Technology Series, and he published articles in technical journals, including IEEE Computer Magazine, IBM Systems Journal, Distributed Computing, Management Directions, and Object Magazine.

In retirement, Earle has flourished in a second career as a poet. His poetry collections are Everything You Love Is New (Redhawk Publications, 2024) and The Way the Rain Works (Sable Books, 2015). He has been nominated for the Pushcart Prize three times and comanages a monthly poetry series at a Chapel Hill, N.C., bookstore. His poems have appeared in many print and online outlets, including The Sun, Carolina Quarterly, and Sufi Journal.

#3227. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3225. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3224. HomeKit Weekly: Airversa’s Humelle is the Thread humidifier my house needs this winter

I love natural gas heat for a few reasons, but one is avoiding AUX heat from a heat pump and watching the bill rise. The downside is when the gas heat kicks on, the air in mt house is bone dry. My nose ends up being super dry for months. A humidifier like the Airversa Humelle works with Apple Home over Thread, so it can run itself based on what the air actually needs, and with the temps in my area getting into the 40s in the next week, I am glad I have one.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Airversa Humelle humidifier uses Thread, so it does join your existing Thread network via a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K and communicates with Apple Home locally. In my experience, Thread accessories always respond faster and drop connections less than Wi-Fi-only ones, and they don’t add to the pile of devices fighting for airtime on your router either. Especially since most smart home devices are 2.4 GHz only.

Once the Airversa Humelle is paired with Apple Home, it appears in the Home app as a humidifier with a built-in temperature and humidity sensor. The latter sensor is the key for automations as well. You can set a target humidity level, and in Auto Mode, it ramps the mist up or down on its own to hold that number. For most people, that’s all the automation they’ll ever need. Set it to 45%, and it’ll run forever. By including that sensor in the device, you don’t need to pair it with a separate Apple Home-compatible humidity sensor for the automations. In fact, that is probably the only automation to run with this device.

The Humelle has a 3.2L tank that Airversa rates at up to 60 hours of runtime, and the mist reaches about 40 inches high, so it covers a bedroom or an average-sized living room pretty easily. It’s a top-fill design, which honestly is the only way these should be made at this point. Flipping them over always ends with some water on the floor.

Sleep Mode runs at 28dB, which is good for a baby’s room, etc. There’s a multicolor LED on the base that you can set to whatever color you want from the Home app or the Sleekpoint app, or turn off completely. There’s also a tray for essential oils if you want it to double as a diffuser to improve a room’s smell.

One thing to know about the Airversa Humelle going in: you’ll still want the Sleekpoint app for a few things, like setting a cleaning reminder that pings you when it’s time to rinse the tank. Day-to-day control lives in Apple Home, but the setup and maintenance features live in the manufacturer’s app. That’s just where Matter is as a protocol right now.

Natural gas heat dries out your inside air, and the Airversa Humelle fixes it. It allows me to avoid regretting my heating choice when I built my house. A humidifier that knows when the air is dry and turns on is the secret sauce. The Humelle does that in Apple Home with Thread, giving you a humidity sensor you can build the rest of your winter automations around. If you need a Thread Border Router, one of the new HomePod mini 2 units is the best to get started.

The Airversa Humelle is available on Amazon and directly from Airversa.

#3222. I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers  Round 1: The Fake PaperCreated with free versions of ChatGPT and GeminiGhost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.Round 2: The AI-Research PaperCreated by the autonomous research system FARSToo many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”Blurred LinesMy homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.Round 2: Using an AI Science EngineFARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. See the AI-Generated Papers Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.

The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?

Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.

To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.

Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.

I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.

My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.

I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.

At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.

What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”

Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.

I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.

1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.

2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.

3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”

4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.

5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.

2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.

3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.

4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.

5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.

→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.

Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?

As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!

In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”

Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.

On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.

These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.

It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.

Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.

Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.

Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.

Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini

Ghost citationsMany references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.Questionable scientific claimsAn expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.Too many acronymsThe expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.

Created by the autonomous research system FARS

Too many preprintsThe references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.Nonsense in a figureOne technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”AI artifactsAnother figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.

There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.

Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.

Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”

My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?

Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.

What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?

Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.

The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”

FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)

Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.

FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.

Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.

With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.

At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.

Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.

“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.

In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.

Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.

“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”

Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?

In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”

Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”

In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”

To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”

Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.

Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.

Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.

Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.

Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.

Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Benjamin Skuse is a professional freelance writer of all things science and technology. Previously, he earned a Ph.D. in applied mathematics from the University of Edinburgh and an M.Sc. in science communication from the University of the West of England. His work has appeared in New Scientist, WIRED, Physics World, Sky & Telescope, Photonics Focus, and many more.

https://r2dssanity.substack.com/p/taking-an-llm-review-or-summary-at?r=3ncgel&utm_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm_medium=webWhat about the problems when human reviewers use AI to summarize papers? Summaries do go wrong, who suffers? That article describes one thread - I think the link is active for 30 days. I understand that editors and reviewers are volunteering time, but uing AI alone to summarize papers without giving authors a chance to present their view point is a genuine problem. Not just for research, anywhere LLM's are used as screening tools.

While I think the premise of the article is valid, I have serious concerns about the use of the fake publications to test the defenses of publication process. Ultimately this results to experimenting on the publishers and reviewers, which is human experimentation (IEEE PSOB 8.1.1.E). Though the article mentions permission from the publisher, there is no clear ethics statement, indicating how far the approval went. As a voluntary reviewer, I would consent to review the merits of scientific work submitted in good faith, but not consent to be a subject of an experiment itself.

Please do not refer to this as "AI slop". It's chatbot slop, from a chatbot trained to talk like a scientist.

BTW, please stop trying to make blockchain happen. It's last year's solution in search of a problem which it never found.

#3221. Prediction: A Stock Market Crash Is Coming. Here's What Dividend Investors Should Do Based on Warren Buffett's Advice

Stocks just had their worst day since April 2025, and valuations sit near a level seen only once before. Here’s how Warren Buffett’s best-known rule applies to your dividend portfolio.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) fell 4.4% on Thursday, its worst day since April 2025, while the Nasdaq slumped 5.5%. That deep sell-off pushed the Nasdaq into correction territory, with it tumbling more than 10% below its recent record.

Nobody knows whether that's the start of something bigger. But it landed in a market already priced for perfection. The S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio recently closed above 41, more than double its long-term average in the high teens. The only other time it has been this high was right before the dot-com bust.

I can't tell you exactly when the next crash might occur. However, the S&P 500 has experienced 13 bear markets (a decline of 20% or more) since 1929. They occur regularly, about every seven years on average, so another one is undoubtedly coming. While the last one was in 2022, that doesn't mean we won't experience another one sooner rather than later, given the currently elevated CAPE ratio. With another crash inevitable, Warren Buffett's most famous advice is the best guide I know for preparing for one. For dividend investors, it boils down to three specific moves.

Buffett's best-known investing rule is: "Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful." He wrote it down in his 1986 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders.

Buffett's rule isn't to try to predict a crash; it's to become more disciplined when the market becomes overly optimistic. A CAPE ratio above 40 suggests that optimism is ruling the day.

Here's the part dividend investors won't want to miss. Greed isn't limited to AI stocks. It shows up in "safe" dividend payers, too. Coca-Cola (KO -0.06%), one of Buffett's best-known holdings, has surged 40% over the past year. That puts it at a very rich valuation, trading at nearly 29 times earnings, well above the S&P 500's 23.5 times earnings. While Coca-Cola is a premium company, that's still very expensive.

Here are three practical ways dividend investors can heed Buffett's rule of being fearful when others are greedy, so that you can be greedy when others are fearful.

Dividend stocks tend to be more resilient investments. We've seen that during prior stock market crashes. For example, when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the S&P 500 experienced a 47% crash over the next two years. High-quality dividend stocks, on the other hand, delivered much better performance. S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats® (the term Dividend Aristocrats® is a registered trademark of Standard & Poor's Financial Services LLC) gained 4.7% during that period, outperforming the market by a whopping 51.4%. Dividend Aristocrats® also outperformed the S&P 500 during the global financial crisis (-55% to -47.2%). However, they don't always outperform during bear markets (-1.4% underperformance during the COVID crash of 2020).

The lesson is that while dividend stocks typically hold up well during a crash, that's not always the case. It's why investors should avoid buying dividend stocks at premium prices in today's market.

Just because another crash is inevitable isn't a reason not to dump your best dividend stocks. The goal isn't to guess the top; it's to be ready when prices change.

Start building cash by holding off on new purchases at stretched valuations (including dividend reinvestment) and put together your watch list, so you're ready for the next crash. The key to following Buffett's advice is to be disciplined now so that you can view a future crash not as a time to be fearful but as a time to get greedy.

Matt DiLallo has positions in Berkshire Hathaway and Coca-Cola. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Berkshire Hathaway and S&P Global. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3220. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

#3219. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.
